claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential can substantially reduce the computational cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
Training selectively on ab initio molecular-dynamics snapshots of both solid and liquid phases can retain fidelity to ab initio phase free energies.
The learned potential can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonic contributions, and electron–vibration coupling in the calculated free energies.
The proposed target is a multicomponent high-entropy alloy containing up to five principal elements, considered in both solid and molten states near melting.
The training configurations will span solid–liquid transition regimes and be iteratively refined through active learning.
Active learning over transition configurations will allow the potential to accurately capture both solid and liquid phases.
Ab initio configurations can provide adequate coverage of vibrational and electronic degrees of freedom for this purpose.
The intended temperature domain is approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the alloy melting temperature.
A local chemical-environment representation can incorporate electron–phonon coupling and anharmonic vibrational contributions from the training data.
A machine-learning potential can learn DFT-level energies and forces for multicomponent alloy configurations.
Learning the energy landscape and forces for both crystalline and liquid configurations enables efficient free-energy assessment.
The resulting fusion-property predictions will have near-ab initio accuracy.
The method will be at least one order of magnitude faster than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
The method will achieve free-energy fidelity of a few meV per atom.
The proposed demonstration domain extends through quinary alloys with melting points below approximately 2000–2500 K.
Application to alloys beyond the stated compositional domain or to extreme temperature–pressure conditions requires additional validation.
Insufficient or unrepresentative training data can cause systematic free-energy errors.
Unanticipated many-body mechanisms at extreme conditions can cause systematic errors in the learned potential.
The method is falsified if its free energies differ from converged ab initio or TOR-TILD references by more than 5 meV per atom, or if derived thermodynamic properties differ by more than 2%.
